summary: Failure modes generated and agreement-checked from 60 traces.

codes.name: Output_Truncation_Due_To_Token_Limit
codes.description: The agent's output ends abruptly due to hitting the maximum token limit, resulting in content that is demonstrably incomplete at the point of cutoff. Observable indicators include: (1) a diff or patch block that opens with '---', '+++', or '@@' markers but never closes or completes all hunks; (2) a code block that opens with a fence (e.g. triple backtick) but never closes it; (3) a sentence, list item, or line that terminates without punctuation or logical conclusion mid-word or mid-token; (4) a JSON, XML, or structured object with unclosed brackets/tags at the final character of output; or (5) an explicit system-level message such as '[truncated]', 'max tokens reached', or equivalent. The truncation must occur at the END of the output — content missing from the MIDDLE of a response is not this code.
codes.when_to_use: Use A.1 when ALL of the following are true: (a) the final characters of the agent output show one or more of the observable truncation indicators listed above; (b) there is no closing statement, summary, or sign-off after the incomplete content — the output simply stops; (c) the incompleteness is at the structural or syntactic level (e.g. an open code block, an unfinished hunk), not merely a matter of the agent choosing not to elaborate. Also apply A.1 as a SECONDARY code when A.8 (Looping Output) is the primary code and that loop also exhausts the token budget.
codes.when_not_to_use: Do NOT use A.1 when: (1) the output is short or minimal but syntactically complete — brevity alone is not truncation; (2) the agent explicitly states it is stopping early, summarising, or deferring the rest ('I will show the remaining changes in the next step') — this is intentional omission, not token-limit truncation; (3) content appears to be missing from the middle of a response rather than the end; (4) the patch or diff is incorrect or malformed due to a logic error rather than being cut off mid-generation; (5) the response ends with a complete sentence or code block even if the overall task is unfinished — task incompleteness is coded elsewhere (e.g. B-series codes), not here.

codes.name: Wrong_File_Targeted
codes.description: An agent generates a patch targeting a file path that does not exist in the repository, uses an incorrect path, or targets a file that is not the one containing the bug, causing git to report 'No such file or directory' or the patch to be applied to the wrong location entirely. The failure locus is file-path identity, not line-content identity.
codes.when_to_use: When the file path in the diff header does not exist in the repository, or exists but is demonstrably not the file that contains the bug being addressed.
codes.when_not_to_use: When the file path is correct but the context lines within it are wrong (use A.13); when retrieval failed to surface the correct file and the agent had no information about it (also consider A.12 as contributing cause).

codes.name: Instruction_Noncompliance
codes.description: An agent ignores, contradicts, or incompletely follows the directives in its system prompt or task instructions — such as producing output in the wrong format, addressing a different problem than specified, omitting required output sections, or violating explicit constraints (e.g., 'do not modify test files', 'output only a unified diff'). The agent received the instructions but did not adhere to them.
codes.when_to_use: When the agent's output violates an explicit instruction present in the system prompt or task specification — wrong output format, wrong problem addressed, prohibited actions taken, required sections missing.
codes.when_not_to_use: When the instruction was never delivered due to a handoff failure (use A.4); when the agent explicitly refused the instruction (use A.7); when the output format is correct but the content is factually wrong (use a content-quality code); when context overflow caused the instructions to be silently dropped (use A.3).

codes.name: Tool_Or_API_Interaction_Failure
codes.description: An agent makes an incorrect or malformed call to an external tool or API — such as invoking the wrong tool, passing incorrect arguments, misinterpreting a tool's response, or failing to handle a tool error — resulting in the agent operating on bad data, missing information, or producing output based on a failed tool interaction. Covers both the call failure itself and downstream errors caused by misreading a valid tool response.
codes.when_to_use: When an agent's tool call log shows a malformed request, an error response from a tool that was not handled, wrong arguments passed to a tool, or when the agent's subsequent reasoning demonstrably misinterprets a tool's returned output.
codes.when_not_to_use: When the tool call was correct and the tool itself had an infrastructure failure outside agent control; when the agent never attempted to call a tool it should have (use A.7 or A.15 if instruction-driven); when retrieval-specific failures occur at the BM25 stage (use A.12).

codes.name: Context_Window_Overflow_Causing_Information_Loss
codes.description: The input to an agent exceeds or approaches the context window capacity, causing early retrieved content, issue details, or prior reasoning to be silently dropped or truncated before the model processes the prompt. The agent receives a degraded view of the task. Distinguished from A.4: A.3 is a passive capacity failure (content was fetched but dropped due to length), not a structural handoff omission. Disambiguation: if the file was never retrieved, code A.12; if the file was retrieved but dropped from the prompt due to length, code A.3.
codes.when_to_use: When the prompt input length approaches or exceeds the model's context window limit and required information (files, issue text, prior reasoning) is silently absent from the agent's effective input.
codes.when_not_to_use: When information was never retrieved in the first place (use A.12); when a structural handoff serialization or templating error omitted content that fit within the window (use A.4); when the output — not input — is truncated (use A.1).

codes.name: Inter_Agent_Handoff_Information_Loss
codes.description: Apply this code when you can produce a literal side-by-side diff between (a) the upstream agent's final output artifact (log line, return value, serialized object) and (b) the downstream agent's received input artifact (log line, prompt text, deserialized object), AND that diff reveals at least one of these specific discrepancies: a field present upstream is absent downstream; a string value is shorter downstream than upstream; a variable that was populated upstream arrives as null, empty string, or a placeholder token downstream; or a numeric/boolean value differs between the two artifacts without any intentional transformation. Additionally, you must identify by name the specific code-level mechanism responsible — e.g., 'the extract_output() regex on line 42 failed to capture the JSON key results', 'the Jinja prompt template omits the {{context}} variable on tool calls', or 'the message queue serializer drops keys with null values'. All three checkpoints must be confirmed: (1) the diff artifact exists and shows a concrete difference, (2) the upstream artifact was captured AFTER the agent completed its final output step and BEFORE any handoff function was called, confirming the content was correct at source, (3) a token-count or character-count check confirms the full upstream content is below the downstream model's context limit, ruling out model-level truncation.
codes.when_to_use: Use this code ONLY when ALL of the following are true and each is directly evidenced: (1) You have retrieved and can cite two discrete log or text artifacts — one from immediately after the upstream agent finishes and one from immediately before the downstream agent begins — and a character- or field-level diff between them is non-empty. (2) You can name a single, specific handoff mechanism (a function name, a template file, a serialization call, a regex, a message schema) as the proximate cause of the discrepancy seen in the diff. (3) A token count of the upstream output confirms it fits within the downstream model's published context window, so model truncation is ruled out. (4) The missing or altered content was semantically necessary for the downstream task — not metadata, comments, or debug fields.
codes.when_not_to_use: Do NOT use this code in any of the following situations: (a) You only have the downstream agent's input and must infer what the upstream agent produced — actual upstream output artifact is unavailable. (b) The discrepancy could be explained by an intentional transformation, summarization, or formatting step that is documented in the pipeline design. (c) The upstream agent itself produced incomplete or incorrect output before handoff (that is an upstream agent error code, not a handoff error). (d) The content difference is limited to whitespace, punctuation normalization, or encoding changes that do not alter semantic meaning. (e) The missing content exceeds the downstream model's context window, making model-level truncation a plausible alternative cause. (f) You can identify that a discrepancy exists but cannot name the specific mechanism responsible — vague attributions such as 'something in the pipeline dropped it' do not qualify. (g) The two artifacts being compared were not captured at the correct boundary points (immediately post-upstream-output and immediately pre-downstream-input), making the diff potentially contaminated by other pipeline steps.

codes.name: Agent_Refusal_Or_Task_Abandonment
codes.description: An agent declines to produce the required output or abandons the task partway through, returning a refusal message, an explanation of why it cannot proceed, or an empty/null output in place of the expected artifact. This includes safety-triggered refusals, capability disclaimers, and mid-task stops where partial output is returned with an explicit statement that the agent will not continue.
codes.when_to_use: When the agent explicitly states it cannot or will not complete the task, or when the output is an explanation/apology rather than the requested artifact.
codes.when_not_to_use: When output is produced but truncated without an explicit refusal (use A.1); when the pipeline itself stops rather than the agent declining (use A.10); when the agent produces output but it is wrong (use appropriate content-quality code).

codes.name: Repetitive_Or_Looping_Output
codes.description: An agent generates pathologically repetitive content — repeating the same lines, hunks, reasoning steps, or phrases in a loop — consuming the output budget without producing useful progress. When the looping also exhausts the token limit, A.8 is coded as the primary failure (root cause) and A.1 as a secondary consequence, to avoid attributing the truncation to a standalone token-limit event.
codes.when_to_use: When the output contains the same content block repeated two or more times with no functional variation, indicating a generation loop rather than intentional repetition.
codes.when_not_to_use: When output is truncated but there is no evidence of repetition before the cutoff (use A.1 alone); when the repetition is a legitimate part of the patch (e.g., similar fixes applied to multiple locations).

codes.name: Unvalidated_Final_Output_Silent_Failure
codes.description: The pipeline emits a final patch as its output without any validation pass having been applied to it — meaning a still-broken, non-applying, or malformed patch is returned as the result with no error signal. This code applies when validation is structurally absent, misconfigured, or bypassed, regardless of whether the absence was caused by premature termination. When premature pipeline termination is the root cause of the missing validation, A.10 should be coded as primary and A.9 as secondary.
codes.when_to_use: When the final output patch was never processed by the automated checker stage, either because the stage does not exist in the pipeline configuration, was skipped due to a routing error, or was bypassed — and a broken patch was returned without any error being raised.
codes.when_not_to_use: When validation ran but produced a false negative (erroneously passed a bad patch); when premature termination is the root cause of skipped validation (use A.10 as primary, A.9 as secondary); when the patch was validated and correctly flagged but not fixed (different failure).

codes.name: Premature_Pipeline_Termination
codes.description: Premature_Pipeline_Termination applies when a multi-stage agent pipeline stops executing and delivers final output before all architecturally mandatory stages have run, where the stopping is caused by an error, exception, resource failure, or implementation bug rather than any designed exit logic. To apply this code, an annotator must be able to confirm ALL THREE of the following: (1) A pipeline stage definition exists (in config, code, or documentation) that lists N required stages in a fixed or conditional sequence; (2) The execution trace or output log shows that fewer than N stages produced an invocation record or output artifact — meaning at least one named, required stage has zero evidence of having run; (3) The output returned to the user originates from a stage that is not the designated terminal stage, with no explicit early-exit rule (such as a confidence threshold, error-recovery path, or user interrupt) documented as the cause of stopping.
codes.when_to_use: Use this code ONLY when all of the following are simultaneously true and independently verifiable in the artifact being annotated: (a) You can identify a concrete list of required pipeline stages from source code, a config file, or authoritative documentation — not inferred; (b) At least one stage on that list has no invocation record, no output artifact, and no skip/bypass annotation in the execution log; (c) The output presented as final is traceable to a non-terminal stage (e.g., a 'Drafter' stage output is returned when a 'Refiner' and 'Formatter' stage were supposed to follow); (d) No designed conditional exit logic (confidence gate, retry-limit halt, user cancellation signal) is present in the log that would legitimately explain the stop.
codes.when_not_to_use: Do NOT use this code in any of the following situations: (1) The pipeline reached its designated terminal stage and produced output from it, even if earlier stages produced poor-quality or missing outputs; (2) An explicit early-exit condition is documented in the pipeline design (e.g., 'if confidence > 0.95, skip refinement') and that condition was met — this is intentional, not premature; (3) A stage is absent because it is conditionally optional and the condition for skipping it was satisfied; (4) The pipeline definition is ambiguous or unavailable and the stage count cannot be independently confirmed — do not infer pipeline structure from output alone; (5) The termination was caused by a user-issued stop, timeout configured as an accepted exit path, or a documented fallback behavior; (6) Only one stage exists in the pipeline, making the concept of 'premature' inapplicable.

codes.name: Retrieval_Stage_Failure_Causing_Missing_Context
codes.description: The BM25 retrieval stage fails to surface the source file(s) containing the bug, or retrieves entirely irrelevant files, so the downstream agent operates without the necessary source context. This is a retrieval precision/recall failure — the relevant file was never fetched. Distinguished from A.3: if the file was never retrieved, code A.12; if the file was retrieved but subsequently dropped from the prompt due to context window overflow, code A.3.
codes.when_to_use: When retrieval logs confirm that the file containing the bug was not present in the retrieved set, or when retrieved files have no relevance to the reported issue.
codes.when_not_to_use: When the correct file was retrieved but dropped from the prompt due to context overflow (use A.3); when the file was retrieved and included but the agent misread or misunderstood it (use a content-quality code); when retrieval was bypassed due to pipeline termination (use A.10).

codes.name: Diff_Context_Mismatch
codes.description: An agent produces a syntactically valid unified diff, but the context lines (unchanged lines surrounding the edit) do not exactly match the actual file content at the targeted location, causing git apply or patch to fail with a 'context mismatch' or 'hunk failed' error. The file path is correct and the edit intent may be correct, but the surrounding lines diverge from the real file state.
codes.when_to_use: When git apply fails with a hunk-level error, the targeted file exists and the path is correct, but the context lines in the diff do not match the current file content at the specified location.
codes.when_not_to_use: When the file path itself is wrong or the file does not exist (use A.14); when the diff is syntactically malformed rather than contextually mismatched; when the patch applies cleanly but produces incorrect behavior.

codes.name: Solver_Wrong_File_Patched
codes.description: Solver applies the fix to an incorrect file path — either a file not containing the bug, a related but wrong module, or a file path that does not exist in the repository. The patch may apply cleanly but modifies the wrong artifact, leaving the actual bug untouched.
codes.when_to_use: When the solver's diff targets a file path that is not the file responsible for the reported bug — including nonexistent paths, sibling modules, or test files instead of source files.
codes.when_not_to_use: When the correct file is patched but additional files also needed changes (use B.2). When the file path is correct but the diff itself is structurally invalid (use B.5). When the file is correct but the logic of the fix is wrong (use B.7).

codes.name: Solver_Incomplete_Fix_Missing_Locations
codes.description: Solver correctly identifies and fixes the bug in one location but fails to apply equivalent fixes to other locations in the codebase that contain the same defect pattern. The partial fix may cause some tests to pass while leaving related failure paths unresolved.
codes.when_to_use: When the solver's patch is logically correct for the location it touches, but one or more additional files or code sites with the identical or symmetrical bug are left unpatched.
codes.when_not_to_use: When the single location patched is itself wrong (use B.1). When the logic of the fix at the patched location is incorrect (use B.7). When the missed locations represent a separate, distinct bug rather than the same defect replicated.

codes.name: Solver_Produces_Multiple_Conflicting_Patch_Blocks
codes.description: Solver outputs more than one candidate patch block (e.g., multiple <patch> or <diff> sections with different approaches), creating ambiguity about which patch is authoritative. Automated application systems cannot resolve the conflict and may apply none, the wrong one, or produce a corrupted result.
codes.when_to_use: When the solver's response contains two or more distinct diff or patch sections that propose different, mutually exclusive changes to the same codebase.
codes.when_not_to_use: When multiple hunks exist within a single well-formed unified diff targeting different files or regions (that is normal diff structure). When the solver provides one patch and one explanatory code block that is clearly not intended as a patch.

codes.name: Solver_Malformed_Diff
codes.description: Solver produces a diff that cannot be successfully applied due to authoring errors in the diff itself — including missing or malformed --- /+++ file headers, missing or invalid @@ hunk headers, and context lines that do not exactly match the actual source file content. All such errors share the same failure mode: the patch tool rejects or misapplies the diff regardless of whether the underlying logical intent was correct.
codes.when_to_use: When the solver's diff fails or misapplies at the patch-application stage due to any structural or content mismatch in the diff format: wrong context lines, absent headers, malformed hunk offsets, incorrect line counts, or mixed indentation/whitespace that diverges from the real file. Use a sub-note to record the specific manifestation (e.g., 'wrong context lines', 'missing @@ header').
codes.when_not_to_use: When the diff is structurally valid and applies cleanly but produces a logically incorrect result (use B.7). When the solver produced no diff output at all due to a system-level failure such as a crash or timeout (outside B-code scope). When the wrong file is targeted but the diff format itself is valid (use B.1).

codes.name: Solver_Logically_Incorrect_Fix
codes.description: Solver produces a syntactically valid, cleanly-applying patch that does not correctly fix the reported issue. The fix may address a symptom rather than the root cause, introduce a different bug, handle only a subset of the triggering conditions, or be semantically inverted. The patch passes formatting and application checks but fails to satisfy the correctness requirements of the issue.
codes.when_to_use: When the diff applies without errors and modifies the intended file, but the resulting code does not resolve the reported bug — as evidenced by continued test failures, incorrect logic, incomplete condition handling, or introduction of a new defect.
codes.when_not_to_use: When the patch fails to apply at all due to diff formatting problems (use B.5). When the correct file is not targeted (use B.1). When the fix is correct at the patched site but missing from other required sites (use B.2).

codes.name: Incorrect_Logic_For_Domain_Semantics
codes.description: The patch changes code in a way that is syntactically valid and applies cleanly, but the logic is incorrect given the domain semantics — e.g., using dict merge when replacement is required, incorrect SQL generation logic, wrong field traversal in ORM, or incorrect mathematical/symbolic transformation.
codes.when_to_use: When the reasoning arrives at a logically incorrect fix for the described behavior — the change is coherent code but produces wrong results for the stated use case. This requires the judge to follow the reasoning argument in the trace and identify where the logic diverges from what the issue requires.
codes.when_not_to_use: When the fix is correct but fails to apply due to context mismatch (use C.1). When the fix addresses only part of the problem (use C.4). When the fix targets the wrong location (use C.3).

codes.name: Missing_Import_For_Introduced_Symbol
codes.description: The patch uses a function, class, or module that is not imported in the target file and does not add the necessary import statement, causing a NameError at runtime.
codes.when_to_use: When the diff introduces a call or reference to a name (e.g., sys.exit, warnings.warn, cbook.Grouper) that does not appear in any existing import in the file and no corresponding import line is added by the patch.
codes.when_not_to_use: When the symbol is a builtin, already imported in the file, or the patch correctly includes an import addition. Do not use for missing type annotations.

codes.name: Type_Heterogeneity_Comparison_Error
codes.description: The fix fails to normalize mixed types before comparison or membership testing — e.g., comparing Path objects to str objects, or mixing os.path strings with pathlib.Path instances — so the check silently produces the wrong boolean result.
codes.when_to_use: When the issue explicitly describes a type mismatch (e.g., Path vs str) causing a duplicate or equality check to fail, and the proposed fix either does not normalize both sides or normalizes only one side of the comparison.
codes.when_not_to_use: When the comparison involves a different kind of logic error unrelated to type normalization. Do not use when the types are already homogeneous.

codes.name: Overconstrained_Or_Underconstrained_Condition
codes.description: The patch adds, removes, or rewrites a conditional expression in a way that is either too broad (excluding valid inputs that should pass) or too narrow (allowing invalid inputs that should be rejected). This includes adding a guard that rejects a legitimate edge case, writing a condition that short-circuits before all required checks are evaluated, reordering checks so that a later guard becomes unreachable, or loosening a check so that invalid states pass through. The condition's range of accepted or rejected values does not match the intended semantics.
codes.when_to_use: Use when the patch changes a conditional expression and the new condition's acceptance set is demonstrably wrong — either over-inclusive or under-inclusive — relative to the domain specification or the test cases shown in the trace. This subsumes cases where reordering checks causes one of them to become unreachable or to fire in the wrong order.
codes.when_not_to_use: Do not use for general logic errors not involving a conditional change (use C.3); do not use when the condition is correct but applied at the wrong location (use C.10); do not use when the condition is correct but the method returns the wrong sentinel type (use C.13).

codes.name: Numerical_Precision_Or_Unit_Semantic_Error
codes.description: The patch introduces or preserves an incorrect assumption about numerical precision, floating-point representation, physical units, or coordinate system conventions in a scientific computing context. Examples include using floating-point equality instead of tolerance-based comparison, applying a unit conversion in the wrong direction or at the wrong step, confusing radians with degrees, mixing Cartesian and spherical coordinate representations, or mishandling masked or NaN values in array operations. The fix is logically structured but numerically or physically incorrect given the domain's mathematical semantics.
codes.when_to_use: Use in scientific computing patches (e.g., Astropy, NumPy-based libraries) when the error is specifically about numerical precision handling, unit conversion logic, coordinate transform ordering, or masked/NaN propagation — and not a general Python logic error.
codes.when_not_to_use: Do not use for general logic errors unrelated to numerical or unit semantics (use C.3); do not use when the issue is a type mismatch rather than a unit or precision error (use C.16); do not use for visualization rendering logic errors (use C.21).

codes.name: Rendering_State_Or_Artist_Lifecycle_Error
codes.description: The patch misunderstands the stateful rendering pipeline of a visualization library, producing a fix that incorrectly manages artist objects, axes state, figure lifecycle, or draw/render ordering. Examples include calling draw() before data is set, modifying artist properties after the renderer has already consumed them, adding an artist to the wrong axes, clearing state that must persist across draw calls, or mishandling the relationship between Figure, Axes, and Artist in Matplotlib's object hierarchy.
codes.when_to_use: Use in visualization library patches (e.g., Matplotlib) when the error is specifically about the order of renderer calls, the lifecycle of artist or axes objects, or the propagation of state through the Figure→Axes→Artist hierarchy — not a general Python logic error.
codes.when_not_to_use: Do not use for numerical precision errors in plotted data (use C.20); do not use for general logic errors unrelated to rendering state (use C.3); do not use when the issue is a missing import for a Matplotlib symbol (use C.15).

codes.name: Estimator_Contract_Or_Array_Protocol_Error
codes.description: The patch violates the implicit or explicit contract of a machine learning estimator interface or array protocol. Examples include modifying fit() in a way that prevents predict() from using the learned state, failing to call check_is_fitted() before accessing fitted attributes, mutating input arrays in-place when the contract requires returning a copy, not preserving sample dimension alignment between X and y, or mishandling sparse matrix inputs by applying dense-only operations. The fix is syntactically correct but breaks the estimator or transformer contract expected by the framework.
codes.when_to_use: Use in machine learning library patches (e.g., scikit-learn) when the error is specifically about the fit/transform/predict lifecycle contract, array mutability guarantees, sample-dimension invariants, or sparse-vs-dense input handling — not a general logic error.
codes.when_not_to_use: Do not use for numerical precision errors in model outputs (use C.20); do not use for general logic errors unrelated to the estimator contract (use C.3); do not use when the issue is only a missing import (use C.15).

codes.name: HTTP_Session_Or_Request_Lifecycle_Error
codes.description: The patch mismanages the lifecycle of HTTP sessions, connections, adapters, or request/response objects in an HTTP client library. Examples include closing a session before a response body has been consumed, reusing a connection object across threads without proper locking, failing to drain or release a response body on redirect or retry, incorrectly mutating headers or cookies on a shared session object, or misunderstanding when authentication hooks are applied relative to redirect resolution.
codes.when_to_use: Use in HTTP client library patches (e.g., Requests) when the error is specifically about session or connection lifecycle management, response body consumption ordering, header/cookie mutation on shared objects, or the sequencing of authentication and redirect handling — not a general logic error.
codes.when_not_to_use: Do not use for general logic errors unrelated to HTTP lifecycle (use C.3); do not use when the issue is purely a type mismatch in URL or header values (use C.16); do not use when the fix is at the wrong abstraction layer (use C.10).

codes.name: Transaction_Isolation_Or_Connection_State_Error
codes.description: The patch incorrectly manages database transaction boundaries, connection state, cursor lifecycle, or isolation-level assumptions in a database ORM or driver context. Examples include issuing a query outside an active transaction when one is required, failing to call commit() or rollback() after a state-changing operation, reusing a cursor after it has been closed or exhausted, assuming autocommit behavior when the connection is in manual-transaction mode, or performing schema-altering DDL inside a transaction that the database engine does not support.
codes.when_to_use: Use in database ORM or driver patches when the error is specifically about transaction lifecycle management, connection state assumptions, cursor reuse, or DDL-in-transaction constraints — not a general query logic error (use C.3 for wrong ORM query semantics).
codes.when_not_to_use: Do not use for incorrect ORM query construction or field traversal errors (use C.3); do not use when the issue is purely a schema migration ordering problem (use C.3 with migration context); do not use for general logic errors unrelated to transaction or connection state (use C.3).

codes.name: Reasoning_Abandoned_Before_Valid_Patch
codes.description: The reasoning process produces partial analysis or a prose description of the fix but stops short of generating a complete, valid unified diff — outputting commentary, pseudocode, or an incomplete diff instead of the required patch.
codes.when_to_use: When the trace shows reasoning that correctly identifies the fix needed but the final output is not a complete patch — e.g., outputs 'But it should be:' with no following diff, outputs analysis only, or outputs a diff that is cut off.
codes.when_not_to_use: When a complete diff is produced but fails to apply (use C.1 or C.2). When the reasoning is complete but logically wrong (use C.9).

codes.name: Context_Line_Content_Mismatch
codes.description: The patch's context lines (unchanged lines used for locating the hunk) do not exactly match the actual file content — differing in whitespace, indentation, wording, or surrounding code — causing the patch tool to fail when applying the hunk.
codes.when_to_use: When the trace shows git/patch reporting 'hunk failed', 'malformed patch at line N', or 'N out of N hunks ignored', and inspection reveals the context lines in the diff do not match the actual source file content.
codes.when_not_to_use: When the failure is caused by wrong file headers (--- /+++) or missing @@ markers rather than incorrect context line content. Do not use when the patch applies cleanly.

codes.name: Malformed_Diff_Format
codes.description: The output is not a valid unified diff: it is missing required --- /+++ file headers, @@ hunk markers, or contains non-diff prose mixed into the patch body.
codes.when_to_use: When the automated check explicitly states 'The output does not look like a unified diff' or 'missing --- /+++ headers', or when the trace shows explanatory text, XML tags, or narrative prose interspersed with or replacing the patch.
codes.when_not_to_use: When the diff has correct headers/markers but context lines are wrong (use C.1 instead). Do not use when the patch is structurally valid even if it applies to the wrong location.

codes.name: Wrong_Fix_Location_Or_Layer
codes.description: The fix is applied to a different file, function, or abstraction layer than where the bug actually originates, so the root cause remains unaddressed even if the patch applies cleanly.
codes.when_to_use: When the reasoning targets a symptom location rather than the causal location, or patches a helper/utility when the real bug is in the caller (or vice versa), or patches one file when the issue description clearly points to another.
codes.when_not_to_use: When the correct file is patched but the context lines are wrong (use C.1). Do not use when multiple locations legitimately need patching (use C.4 instead).

codes.name: Incomplete_Fix_Missing_Callsites
codes.description: The patch corrects the bug at one location but omits one or more additional locations in the codebase that exhibit the same pattern or require the symmetric change, leaving the issue partially unresolved.
codes.when_to_use: When the issue description or codebase clearly contains multiple analogous patterns (e.g., multiple yield sites, multiple branches, symmetric API methods) and the patch addresses only a subset of them.
codes.when_not_to_use: When there is only one relevant location to fix, or when the unpatched locations are deliberately out of scope. Do not use for format/structure errors.

codes.name: Symptom_Suppression_Instead_Of_Root_Cause_Fix
codes.description: The patch masks or works around the visible symptom (e.g., catching an exception and silently ignoring it, adding a no-op comment, guarding with an unnecessary hasattr check) without addressing the underlying defect that causes the symptom.
codes.when_to_use: When the fix does not change program logic in a way that eliminates the root cause, but instead prevents the symptom from surfacing — e.g., adding a noqa comment to silence an error, wrapping in a try/except without correction, or adding a guard that hides the problem.
codes.when_not_to_use: When the fix genuinely corrects the root cause even if it appears minimal. Do not use when the added check is a legitimate protocol requirement.

codes.name: Wrong_Sentinel_Or_Return_Value_Type
codes.description: A dunder method or protocol hook raises an exception (e.g., ValueError, NotImplementedError) or returns a wrong type where the protocol requires a specific sentinel value (e.g., returning NotImplemented so Python can try the reflected operation).
codes.when_to_use: When a patch modifies a dunder method (__array_ufunc__, __eq__, __add__, etc.) and raises an exception instead of returning NotImplemented, or returns a truthy/falsy value where a specific sentinel is mandated by the Python data model.
codes.when_not_to_use: When the method is not a dunder/protocol method, or when raising is explicitly the correct behavior for that protocol. Do not use for general incorrect return values outside protocol methods.

codes.name: Duplicate_Code_Insertion
codes.description: The patch introduces a duplicate definition of an existing symbol — re-declaring a variable, re-defining a function or class, or re-inserting a block of code that already exists nearby — resulting in shadowing, redefinition, or doubled logic.
codes.when_to_use: When the diff adds a line or block that already exists in the file at the same or nearby scope, creating a second definition or declaration of the same identifier.
codes.when_not_to_use: When the new definition intentionally replaces (via removal of the old) rather than duplicates the existing one. Do not use for adding a new overload or subclass.
